ex_sub: See which features the model relies on and why it decided what it did for one sample.
ex_none: No saved model yet. Run the Pipeline Runner with hold-out enabled and the model will appear here.
ex_intro: A detector that scores high is only useful if it relies on sensible evidence. This page answers two questions: which features does the model depend on overall, and which features pushed it to its decision for one particular sample.
ex_global_help: A longer bar means the model depends more on that feature.
ex_axis_perm: Drop in macro F1 when the feature is shuffled (points)
ex_perm_note: Permutation importance shuffles one feature at a time on held-out test samples and measures how much the model gets worse. It is computed on up to 500 test samples.
ex_nar_none: No feature changes the model's accuracy when shuffled, so the importance cannot be ranked on this sample. Try another model or run.
ex_nar_top: The {n} features the model depends on most are {names}.
ex_nar_conc: Most of the decision rests on one feature, {f} ({s:.0f}%). If this feature is derived from the label (for example an antivirus detection score), the high accuracy may be overstated. Check it with a run that excludes it.
ex_nar_spread: The importance is spread over many features (the top 5 hold {s:.0f}%), so the model combines many weak signals instead of relying on one.
ex_nar_top5: The top 5 features hold {s:.0f}% of the importance, so a small group of features drives most decisions.
ex_nar_unused: {n} of {total} features do not change the result at all and could be dropped.
ex_nar_agree: The model's own importance agrees with permutation ({k} of the top 5 are shared), which makes the ranking more trustworthy.
ex_nar_differ: The model's own importance and permutation disagree ({k} of the top 5 are shared). Treat the ranking with caution; correlated features often split importance between them.
ex_local_help: Pick one test sample. Each bar shows how much the predicted class loses confidence when that feature is replaced by a typical value.
ex_no_wrong: This model made no mistakes on the saved test samples.
ex_wrong_note: The model got this sample wrong. Look at which features pushed it toward the wrong class.
ex_loc_pos: These features pushed the model toward {c}: {f}.
ex_loc_none: No single feature has a clear effect on this sample; the decision comes from many small contributions.
ex_loc_neg: These features pulled against that decision: {f}.
ex_local_note: Effects are measured one feature at a time among the 15 most important features, so they are an approximation.
ex_ai_title: Ask an AI to explain this (optional)
ex_ai_help: Copy the text below into any AI chat (a free tier is enough) to get a plain-language explanation. The page itself does not send anything anywhere.
ex_ai_prompt:
I trained a malware detector. Dataset: {ds}. Model: {m}. Classes: {cl}. Number of features: {n}.
The most important features and their share of importance:
{lines}
Explain in simple language what this tells me about what the model relies on, whether any feature looks suspicious (for example derived from the label), and what I should check next.
ex_how:
**Permutation importance**: shuffle one feature and see how much the model gets worse. A big drop means the model needs that feature.

**Built-in importance**: the model's own count of how useful a feature was while training. It exists only for tree models and linear models.

**Effect on one sample**: replace one feature by a typical value and see how the model's confidence changes. Green bars support the decision, red bars oppose it.

**Caution**: importance shows what the model uses, not what causes malware. Features that are strongly correlated can share the credit.
pr_sub: Apply a saved model to a new CSV file and get a prediction for every row.
pr_expect: This model expects {n} features and predicts: {c}.
pr_hint: Upload a CSV. Columns are matched to the model's features by name; you can fix unmatched ones by hand.
pr_manual_help: Choose which column of your file corresponds to each missing feature, most important first. Leave a feature unmatched to fill it with 0.
pr_manual_more: {n} more features are not shown and will be filled with 0.
pr_err_cov: Fewer than half of the model's features were found in this file, so the prediction would not be meaningful.
pr_err_cov_hint: Columns in your file begin with: {cols}. Rename them or match them by hand above.
pr_fill_note: {n} features are missing and will be filled with 0 (no activity).
pr_warn_w: The matched columns cover less than 70% of what the model relies on. Treat the predictions with caution.
pr_label_help: Choose the label column to check the predictions against the real labels.
pr_bad_cells: {n} cells were not valid numbers and were treated as 0.
pr_low_conf: {n} rows have confidence below 60%; review them first.
pr_acc_note: Computed against the label column you chose.
pr_show_n: Showing {n} of {total} rows. The download contains all rows.
sus_sub: Rate how usable this tool is. Ten short statements, about two minutes.
sus_intro: The System Usability Scale (SUS) is a standard 10-statement questionnaire. Each answer is 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree). The result is a score from 0 to 100; about 68 is the average across many systems.
sus_thanks: Thank you. Your SUS score is {s:.1f}.
sus_q1: I think that I would like to use this system frequently.
sus_q2: I found the system unnecessarily complex.
sus_q3: I thought the system was easy to use.
sus_q4: I think that I would need the support of a technical person to be able to use this system.
sus_q5: I found the various functions in this system were well integrated.
sus_q6: I thought there was too much inconsistency in this system.
sus_q7: I would imagine that most people would learn to use this system very quickly.
sus_q8: I found the system very cumbersome to use.
sus_q9: I felt very confident using the system.
sus_q10: I needed to learn a lot of things before I could get going with this system.
sus_bench: The dashed line is 68, the average SUS score across many systems. With only a few respondents the mean is a rough indication.
